content: 1. This guide was created to support asthma program staff within state health departments (SHDs) in the development and implementation of asthma control programs. 2. Effective asthma program development requires collaboration with local health organizations, medical societies, state or local government entities, managed care organizations, and other stakeholders involved in asthma management, particularly within local communities. 3. The guide outlines evidence-based components of an asthma program, which have been successfully utilized by CDC asthma grantees who have completed the planning process and are actively implementing their state asthma plans. 4. It is important to note that an asthma program and an asthma plan are not synonymous. 5. An asthma plan is developed based on activities conducted within the SHD’s program, such as data collection and interpretation, forming a statewide coalition, and identifying appropriate interventions. 6. The asthma plan represents a collective commitment from engaged partners across the state to allocate resources and complete activities within a defined timeline and with measurable objectives. 7. As the CDC’s and states’ asthma programs evolve, more insights will emerge regarding the elements of a successful asthma control program. 8. The guidance provided in this document may change as programs develop and as our understanding of asthma improves. 9. However, many state asthma programs have been operational long enough to establish fundamental approaches and methodologies that can assist SHDs that have not yet designed their asthma control strategies. 10. This guide is offered in that spirit, and feedback from SHDs on how to enhance this document is welcomed. 11. The primary audience for this guide includes SHDs applying for or receiving CDC funding for capacity building and asthma plan implementation. 12. SHDs that do not receive CDC asthma program funding may still find elements of the guide useful if their agencies have prioritized asthma as a health concern within their state. 13. Asthma is a highly prevalent health issue in the United States, ranking among the most common chronic conditions and affecting an estimated 20.3 million individuals of all ages and races in 2001. 14. The prevalence of asthma is significantly higher among children compared to adults and among African Americans compared to other racial groups. 15. In 1998, asthma accounted for over 2 million emergency department visits, approximately 423,000 hospitalizations, and 5,438 deaths in the United States. 16. Children with asthma miss, on average, twice as many school days as their peers, with 21% of children in one study population missing over two weeks of school annually due to asthma. 17. The estimated direct and indirect monetary costs of asthma totaled $12.7 billion in 1998. 18. Much of the disability and disruption caused by asthma is preventable, as effective treatments are available. 19. A critical concern is identifying individuals with poorly controlled asthma and ensuring they receive appropriate care. 20. Another concern is the lack of awareness among some individuals that they have asthma, despite experiencing significant symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and difficulty breathing, which could benefit from medical intervention. 21. Reducing the burden of asthma requires identifying affected individuals, providing high-quality medical care, implementing environmental modifications, offering supportive outreach services, and assisting patients in adhering to their management regimens. 22. Since asthma is a chronic disease requiring substantial behavioral changes by patients, families, and providers, public health interventions are likely to be beneficial. 23. The integration of appropriate treatment and behavioral change necessitates a melding of clinical care with public and community health practices, which can be facilitated through broad partnerships. 24. Surveillance is essential for understanding disease patterns, planning, and evaluating programs, and SHDs should play a significant role in these efforts. 25. The federal government has recognized the seriousness of asthma and its impact on the quality of life of affected individuals. 26. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) has developed strategic guidelines that shape the CDC’s asthma program goals and provide a framework for state agencies to establish their asthma program infrastructure. 27. The Healthy People 2010 initiative presents a comprehensive, nationwide health promotion and disease prevention agenda, including a chapter dedicated to respiratory diseases with objectives to reduce asthma-related mortality and morbidity and improve patient care quality. 28. Building on the strategic vision of Healthy People 2010, DHHS developed the Action Against Asthma initiative, which outlines a research strategy to uncover the causes of the asthma epidemic and develop prevention methods. 29. The CDC’s asthma program aims to reduce the burden of asthma through improved application of medical and environmental management knowledge. 30. The program includes three main components: surveillance, assistance with science-based interventions, and development of partnerships with key agencies and organizations. 31. Surveillance efforts involve building SHD capacity to collect and evaluate asthma data, implementing telephone surveys, and analyzing national data on asthma prevalence and control. 32. The program also supports states and communities in identifying and implementing evidence-based asthma interventions and expanding the science base through research and demonstration projects. 33. Partnerships with federal and state agencies, healthcare providers, and nonprofit organizations are integral to the program’s success. 34. A commitment to addressing population disparities through culturally relevant interventions and community-based efforts is embedded in all program components. 35. 36. Effective asthma program staffing begins with identifying necessary skills and competencies and matching them to available positions within the SHD’s human resource infrastructure. 37. Program management typically involves individuals with expertise in budget management, administration, and supervision, who oversee policy development, grant implementation, and data evaluation. 38. Epidemiology and surveillance roles require skills in data analysis, designing data collection mechanisms, and interpreting data to guide program planning. 39. 40. Statewide partnerships and coalitions are essential for addressing the complexities of asthma diagnosis, management, and surveillance. 41. Internal partnerships within state agencies and external collaborations with diverse organizations are critical for a successful asthma program. 42. Diversity and inclusivity should be foundational principles in developing statewide partnerships and asthma plans, ensuring representative and participatory processes. 43. Interventions should be data-driven, science-based, and designed to achieve measurable objectives, with evaluation as a core component. 44. School environments offer promising opportunities for asthma interventions, addressing issues such as absenteeism, indoor air quality, and access to medications. 45. Surveillance data should guide intervention planning, focusing on priority audiences and evidence-based methods. 46. Even unsuccessful interventions can provide valuable insights if properly evaluated, contributing to program improvement and strengthened partnerships.
